pages.body: Academy | People for Animals Every drive, camp and open day is free to attend ✕ Academy Animal healthcare, made legible. Medicines, vaccines, antivenom and first aid, written for India. Every lesson shows you its point up front. Open it only if you want the rest. 76 lessons Every claim cited Checked against sources, September 2026 If it is happening right now What is in front of you? 01 Is it an emergency? The sixty-second check Lesson G2 02 Hit by a vehicle Moving a possible broken back Lesson G3 03 Bleeding or a wound Including maggot wounds Lesson G4 04 Snakebite What helps, what harms Lesson E4 05 Poisoning Rat poison, insecticide, medicines Lesson G7 06 Collapsed in the heat Cool first, transport second Lesson G6 If it is you rather than the animal: bitten or scratched yourself, Lesson F2 , or holding a prescription to check, Lesson H4 . None of this replaces a vet. It is what to do in the minutes before you reach one. Find the nearest PFA unit Read this first This is information, not treatment. Every dose on this page is a published label range, shown so that you can read a prescription and catch an arithmetic error, not so that you can write one. In India a medicine marked Rx (Schedule H or H1) is sold only against a registered practitioner's prescription, and veterinary medicine may be practised only by a registered veterinary practitioner. Where a lesson says "vet now", it means the nearest veterinary hospital, college clinic or registered vet, today, not tomorrow. Watch The biology underneath Short films that sit beside the modules, made by other people and credited to them. They play here, with the same controls as the rest of the site. The syllabus Ten modules, in the order a rescuer meets them. Seventy-six lessons across the ten. Each lesson shows its key point without being opened; the detail, the tables and the sources are one tap further in. Search or filter to pull a single topic out of the whole. 01 Foundations: how to read a medicine Generic names, strengths, Schedule H, routes, why a cat is not a small dog, and how to store medicine in Indian heat. 7 lessons 12 min 02 Medicines: the classes you will meet Painkillers, steroids, dewormers, tick and flea products, gut drugs, fluids, hormones, and the street-dog conditions of India. 8 lessons 16 min 03 Antibiotics and resistance What they do and do not touch, the classes on Indian prescriptions, the five rules of a course, and the laws that now govern them. 7 lessons 14 min 04 Vaccines Dogs, cats, community dogs, cattle and buffalo, goats and sheep, horses: the Indian schedules, the cold chain, and why vaccines fail. 9 lessons 18 min 05 Antivenom and snakebite The Big Four, what Indian polyvalent antivenom neutralises, how dose is decided, and the first aid that helps rather than harms. 7 lessons 12 min 06 Immunoglobulins: borrowed immunity Rabies immunoglobulin and monoclonals, antivenom, tetanus antitoxin, colostrum, and why puppy vaccines are a series. 7 lessons 12 min 07 First aid: the first hour Approach, the sixty-second check, road accidents, wounds and maggots, heatstroke, poisoning, burns, newborns, cattle emergencies, the kit. 14 lessons 28 min 08 Dosages: the arithmetic Milligrams per kilogram, tablets and millilitres, the decimal point, a checker for the prescription in your hand, and a reference table. 7 lessons 16 min 09 Indications, contraindications, interactions What a drug is for, when it must not be given, which pairs fight, and how food and timing change a dose. 6 lessons 14 min 10 Do's and Don'ts The essential list, an audit of kitchen remedies from turmeric to Dettol, and the ten sentences that get a vet to help you fast. 4 lessons 10 min All lessons Foundations Medicines Antibiotics Vaccines Antivenom Immunoglobulins First aid Dosages Interactions Do's & Don'ts Expand all Showing every lesson that rests on Clear PFA Academy Foundations: how to read a medicine Most harm done to animals with medicine in India is not done by the wrong drug. It is done by the right drug in the wrong strength, by the wrong route, for the wrong species, or from a bottle that spent a summer in a car. This module gives you the vocabulary to avoid all four. Tell a brand name from the molecule inside it and read a strength off any label. Decode a prescription line, including the abbreviations vets use. Say why a cat, a dog, a cow and a horse each need a different rule book. Store vaccines and medicines so that they still work when needed. 1.1 What is actually in the box: brand, molecule and strength Every medicine has one true name, the generic or molecule name, and any number of brand names. The molecule is what acts; the brand is what the shop stocks. Do this Do this Before giving anything, read three things aloud: the molecule, the strength per tablet or per mL, and the weight of the animal. If any of the three is missing, stop and ask. Meloxicam is meloxicam whether the carton says Melonex, Metacam or a chemist's own brand. The dangerous variable is not the brand but the strength : how many milligrams of the molecule sit in one tablet or one millilitre. Human meloxicam tablets are 7.5 mg and 15 mg. The veterinary oral suspension for dogs is 1.5 mg per mL, and the injection is usually 5 mg per mL. A 5 kg dog on a correct 0.1 mg per kg dose needs 0.5 mg. One human 7.5 mg tablet is fifteen times that. The same is true of the antibiotic amoxicillin-clavulanate, which comes as 375 mg and 625 mg human tablets, veterinary 250 mg and 500 mg tablets, and paediatric syrups of several strengths. Reading "give one tablet" without reading which tablet is how overdoses happen. Basis Merck Vet Manual Plumb's 1.2 Reading an Indian label: Rx, Schedule H, H1, expiry, withdrawal Indian labels carry a small set of legally fixed phrases. Once you can read them, a strip of tablets tells you how it may be bought, how long it lasts and, for a farm animal, how long its milk or meat must be discarded. pages.description: Thirty years of changes People for Animals has made to India’s animal law and to the systems that run it. One hundred and two entries, each naming what changed.
headings: Not what we said. What changed.
Helped end cosmetic testing on animals in India
Secured a ban on the export of shark fins
Advocated for the ban on animal dissection in schools
Delivered frontline veterinary care on the Char Dham route
Put animals into India's disaster response
Pushed States to build real animal-welfare institutions
Stopped the illegal cross-border animal-sacrifice trade at Gadhimai
Care and Maintenance of Case Property Animals Rules, 2017

pages.body: The record | People for Animals Every drive, camp and open day is free to attend ✕ The record Not what we said. What changed. Rules rewritten, orders obtained, practices ended. Thirty years of it, on eight fronts. Every entry below is a thing that is different now because of work that was done, and most of it sits in law rather than in memory. 0 entries in the record 0 fronts worked at once 0 years of it, from 1994 Everything Courts & law Farmed animals Policy & systems Wildlife & shows Community dogs Testing & labs Teaching Working animals 001 Helped end cosmetic testing on animals in India PFA’s campaign contributed to India becoming one of the first countries in the world to prohibit cosmetic testing on animals (2014) and to ban the import of animal-tested cosmetics. Courts & law 2014 002 Secured a ban on the export of shark fins Advocated for an end to shark-fin exports, and in 2015 the Government prohibited the export of shark fins of all species, a ban subsequently upheld in court. Wildlife & shows 2015 003 Protected Rajasthan's camels Campaigned for the camel's recognition as Rajasthan's State Animal and for the 2015 State law prohibiting camel slaughter and regulating their movement and export. Farmed animals 2015 004 Advocated for the ban on animal dissection in schools PFA’s legal and policy action led the Government of India to ban dissection for school students, implemented in 1998. Testing & labs 1998 005 Shaped India's community-dog (ABC) framework Assisted the Government of India to develop the Animal Birth Control Rules of 2001 and 2023, and have supported States and municipalities to implement scientific sterilisation and anti-rabies programmes. Courts & law 2001 006 Delivered frontline veterinary care on the Char Dham route Transformed equine welfare on the Kedarnath Yatra. Since 2024 PFA has delivered veterinary care, health screening and rescue for working equines, by operating an equine infirmary at Rudraprayag. PFA’s advocacy led the Uttarakhand High Court to direct mandatory registration, rest periods, a ban on operations between sunset and sunrise, and mandatory health check of animals before deployment. Courts & law 2024 007 Put animals into India's disaster response After leading the rescue of more than 6,000 animals in the 2013 Uttarakhand floods, PFA assisted the National Disaster Management Authority to develop Animal-Inclusive Disaster Risk Reduction guidelines. Policy & systems 2013 008 Drove reform of laboratory-animal use PFA’s sustained campaign contributed to major reforms in India's laboratory-animal regulation and earned international recognition through the Lush Prize. Testing & labs 009 Pushed States to build real animal-welfare institutions Campaigned nationwide for functional State Animal Welfare Boards, working with every State on the long-pending directive and moving the Supreme Court to require their establishment. Courts & law 010 Helped consumers make informed choices Assisted the Government of India to introduce the mandatory vegetarian and non-vegetarian symbols (red and green dots) on packaged food products. Policy & systems 011 Stopped the illegal cross-border animal-sacrifice trade at Gadhimai In Gauri Maulekhi v. Union of India, PFA moved the Supreme Court, which in 2014 directed authorities to halt the illegal transport of animals across the India–Nepal border for mass sacrifice, establishing a lasting precedent for protecting animals trafficked across international borders. With the Government of Bihar, PFA prevented the trafficking and ritual slaughter of about 700 animals ahead of Nepal's Gadhimai festival, working with the Sashastra Seema Bal from Motihari (30 November–9 December 2024) to intercept smuggling and provide emergency veterinary care. Courts & law 2014 012 Dog Breeding and Marketing Rules, 2017 Obtained directions from the Hon’ble Delhi High Court and assisted the Government of India to develop the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals (Dog Breeding and Marketing) Rules, 2017, creating a national framework for commercial dog breeding and sale. Courts & law 2017 013 Regulation of Livestock Markets Rules, 2017 Obtained directions from the Hon’ble Supreme Court and assisted the Government of India to develop the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals (Regulation of Livestock Markets) Rules, 2017, introducing welfare safeguards for the handling and sale of animals at livestock markets. Courts & law 2017 014 Care and Maintenance of Case Property Animals Rules, 2017 After securing directions from the Hon’ble Supreme Court, PFA assisted the Government of India to develop the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals (Care and Maintenance of Case Property Animals) Rules, 2017, protecting animals seized in cruelty cases during the pendency of proceedings. Courts & law 2017 015 Pet Shop Rules, 2018 Obtained directions from the Hon’ble Delhi High Court and assisted the Government of India to develop the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals (Pet Shop) Rules, 2018, mandating registration and welfare standards for pet shops. Courts & law 2018 016 Environmental rules for dairy farms and gaushalas Advocated, through proceedings before the National Green Tribunal, for stronger environmental regulation of dairy farms and gaushalas, contributing to the Central Pollution Control Board's Guidelines for Environmental Management of Dairy Farms and Gaushalas (2020, revised 2021). Courts & law 2020 017 Environmental rules for poultry farms Advocated, before the National Green Tribunal, for stronger environmental regulation of poultry farms, contributing to the Central Pollution Control Board's Guidelines for Environmental Management of Poultry Farms. Courts & law 018 The Package of Practice for Organised Pig Farms Co-authored the Package of Practice for Organised Pig Farms, with the National Research Center on Pig, Guwahati. This serves as an SOP which promotes welfare of lakhs of pigs and scientific management practices to prevent cruelty. Farmed animals 019 Conditio

pages.title: Careers | People for Animals
pages.description: People for Animals is hiring Zonal Heads: field-based coordinators for its network of Units across India. Two-year term, ₹35,000 a month plus travel. Apply in two minutes.
headings: Which Zone are you applying for?
pages.body: Careers | People for Animals Every drive, camp and open day is free to attend ✕ Careers · one opening Zonal Head. PFA's coordinator for every Unit in a Zone: growing the network, mentoring local leadership, and making sure a cruelty complaint becomes a case that survives prosecution. Field-based. Two years, renewable. ₹35,000 a month plus travel. 9 Zones Full time Apply in about two minutes The role at a glance Title Zonal Head Where Based in the assigned PFA Zone; extensive travel across its States and districts Term Two years, renewable Pay ₹35,000 per month, plus travel Reports to The Chairperson / Principal Organisation Best fit An active working member of a recognised PFA Unit in the Zone, with animal welfare, rescue, NGO, social work or organising experience Apply now Five short screens. People For Animals is India's largest animal welfare organisation, working through a nationwide network of independently registered Units: rescue, shelter and adoption, animal birth control and anti-rabies programmes, cruelty complaints and prosecution, enforcement of animal protection laws, and engagement with government on policy. The Zonal Head is PFA's designated coordinator for all recognised and proposed Units within the assigned Zone. It is a field-based, enforcement- and movement-building role: growing PFA's presence across the Zone, building and mentoring local leadership and volunteers, ensuring an effective animal welfare and enforcement response on the ground, and coordinating with police, veterinary and civic authorities. Each Unit remains independently registered and self-governing; the Zonal Head coordinates and supports them and carries directions from the Principal Organisation. The nine Zones North North : Ladakh, Jammu & Kashmir North : Himachal Pradesh, Punjab, Haryana, Chandigarh Central 1 : Uttar Pradesh Central 2 : Madhya Pradesh, Chhattisgarh East : Bihar, Jharkhand, West Bengal, Odisha North East : Assam, Arunachal Pradesh, Meghalaya, Manipur, Mizoram, Nagaland, Tripura, Sikkim West : Gujarat, Rajasthan, Maharashtra, Goa, Daman and Diu South : Andhra Pradesh, Telangana South South : Kerala, Tamil Nadu, Karnataka What the work is Network and leadership Map the Zone State-wise and district-wise, identify gaps in PFA presence, support new and existing Units, and identify, recommend and mentor local leadership for District and State Units. Build a pipeline of active workers so that no district is left without a first responder. Make PFA Units in each district. Coordination Coordinate with State Coordinators and District Heads, convene review meetings, resolve inter-Unit disputes, and ensure directions from the Principal Organisation are carried out. Animal welfare and enforcement response Prompt, documented action on cruelty, abandonment, injury and neglect complaints: Guide Units in registering complaints and FIRs and in invoking the strongest available provisions. Secure custody of rescued or seized animals as case property under the PCA (Care and Maintenance of Case Property Animals) Rules, 2017, and ensure their care pending trial. Maintain evidentiary discipline: dated photographs and video, witness details, veterinary certificates and a clear chain of custody, so cases survive prosecution rather than collapsing at the complaint stage. Liaise with SHOs, prosecutors, veterinary officers and Honorary Animal Welfare Officers to see cases through to chargesheet and conviction, and track outcomes. Scope of issues (illustrative, not exhaustive) Companion and street animals : dog and cat cruelty, poisoning and culling, feeding disputes with RWAs and authorities, relocation of community animals, ABC gaps. Cattle and large animals : abandoned and stray cattle, gaushala conditions, illegal and cruel transport, unlicensed and cruel slaughter, disease-driven distress. Working animals : equines at brick kilns, tourism sites, weddings and construction; bullocks and draught animals; camels; unfit-to-work animals; lack of water, shade or farriery. Farmed animals : battery cages, live-bird markets, piggeries, cruel handling in transport and markets. Aquatic animals : live fish and seafood transport and market handling; the ornamental fish trade. Wildlife and trade : poaching, snaring and trapping, illegal bird and exotic-pet trade (including CITES-listed species), monkey and parakeet capture, and human–wildlife conflict rescue. Captive and performing animals : captive elephants and temple animals, circuses and unregistered performing animals, roadside menageries, animal-drawn-vehicle abuse. Blood sports and rituals : cockfighting, dog and other animal fighting, bull-taming events, bullock-cart racing, cruelty in religious sacrifice. Seasonal hazards : glass-coated kite string (manja) injuries to birds, festival firecracker distress, heat-wave, cold-wave and monsoon response. Establishments : pet shops (Pet Shop Rules, 2018), dog breeders (Dog Breeding and Marketing Rules, 2017), livestock markets: registration, inspection and closure of illegal operators. Trauma and access to care : road-accident and roadkill response, and access to first aid, ambulances and veterinary treatment. Movement building and community mobilisation Expand the Rapid Response Team app district-wise and drive ABC (per the Animal Birth Control Rules, 2023), anti-rabies vaccination, native and community-dog adoption, sterilisation and vaccination camps, "Be Kind to Animals" outreach and other PFA programmes against measurable district-wise targets. Recruit, train and retain a volunteer and first-responder base in every district; recognise local heroes to sustain morale. Build Animal Welfare Societies on college and school campuses, kept engaged through structured humane-education activities. Support and protect community feeders and caregivers, and mediate neighbourhood conflicts. Build local coalitions with sympathetic veterinarians, lawyers, police officers, RWAs, other NGOs and the media, so PFA's reach outlasts any

pages.title: Founder | People for Animals
pages.description: Maneka Sanjay Gandhi founded People for Animals and built it into India
headings: A circle of love around all life.
What she set out to build.
pages.body: Founder | People for Animals Every drive, camp and open day is free to attend ✕ if the photographer requires one. The gallery images below still point at files hosted on peopleforanimalsindia.org so the page renders complete straight away. Before this goes live, download each one, confirm PFA holds the rights, and re-point the src at a self-hosted copy in /img alongside the portrait. Hot-linking another server's assets breaks the moment they rename a file, and it spends their bandwidth, not yours. Every frame falls back to a labelled placeholder if its source fails, so swapping sources can never leave a broken image on the page. Ideal sizes: portrait 1200x1600 or larger, gallery 1600x1100 or larger. -------------------------------------------------------------------------- --> Founder Maneka Sanjay Gandhi Founder and chairperson of People for Animals. She started the organisation and built it into India s largest animal welfare body, with hospitals, shelters, mobile clinics and members in every part of the country. Compassion without action is evil Smt. Maneka Sanjay Gandhi Smt. Maneka Sanjay Gandhi Founder and chairperson, People for Animals 26 Animal hospitals 90+ PFA units across the country 60 Mobile units on the road 1M+ Lives touched In her words A circle of love around all life. Her argument starts with self-interest, not sentiment. Every species, from bees to elephants, holds up a shield around human life, and the quality of our own lives rests on theirs. Eat them, exploit them, breed one kind while wiping out another, and the damage lands back on us: as each species goes, our own world gets poorer. Her invitation is simply to join the circle of care around all living things. People for Animals turned animal welfare in India from a quiet cause into an organised, assertive movement. Its members are lawyers, film actors, business leaders, civil servants, teachers and students. The work runs from shelters and ambulances through to fighting cases in court, training judges, police officers and bureaucrats, and publishing material that teaches people how to care for animals. Its wins have come in courtrooms, in research laboratories, and at racecourses, temples, circuses and zoos. PFA is now counted among the strongest animal groups anywhere in the world. When the first International Animal Welfare Directory was assembled, its British publishers asked PFA to write the foreword. In 2001 the first Padma Shri awarded in this field went to a PFA member, Dr Norma Alvares. What she set out to build. The strategy behind the organisation, and the target it still works towards: an animal welfare centre in every district in India, of which there are now about 800. 01 Create infrastructure Build and upgrade the physical means of rescue: shelters, ambulances, mobile clinics and helplines that answer when someone finds an injured animal. 02 Influence policy Work as a pressure group for legislation that protects animals and the environment, rather than waiting for it to arrive on its own. 03 Make the law bite Take direct action through PFA units nationwide, so that animals are protected in practice and offenders actually face consequences. 04 Educate and sensitise Animal welfare groups in schools and colleges, training for lawyers, police, the judiciary and civil servants, and published guides on animal care. 05 Advance the movement Work alongside Indian and international welfare groups, fund initiatives that deserve it, and open real career paths in animal welfare. 06 Change what we eat Make the health, environmental and economic case for plant-based choices, and find and promote alternatives that use no animals at all. Watch Her, in motion. Nothing loads from Facebook or Instagram until you press play, so the page stays fast and sets no third-party cookies before you ask. Carry it on Compassion, then action. The organisation she started runs on gifts from people who will never meet the animals they help. A single gift covers food, treatment and a place to sleep for an animal who had none of the three this morning. Donate Find your nearest unit Instagram Close Open on Instagram

pages.description: Plain-language answers on animal law in India, applicable in every State: dogs, cattle, husbandry and working equines.
headings: Breed bans have no legal footing
PCA penalties are still token, so do not stop there
pages.body: Laws | People for Animals Every drive, camp and open day is free to attend ✕ Laws What the law actually says. Answers on animal law in India, written to hold in every State. Where the law is a State subject the answer says so and tells you what to look up locally. Every answer names the provision it rests on, because a complaint that cites the section is far harder to refuse than one that does not. Every answer cited Updated August 2026 Before you cite any of this Every answer names the provision it rests on, so you can check it rather than take it on trust. Read the section on indiacode.nic.in before you quote it, and check your State: prevention of cruelty is a concurrent subject, so State rules and municipal by-laws sit on top of everything here. A section cited wrongly in an FIR is harder to correct than one left out. Last read against the statutes in August 2026. All Dogs Cattle Husbandry Equines Expand all Showing every question that rests on Clear Dogs A1 Which law protects dogs from cruelty? Two provisions, always read together. Section 3 of the PCA Act 1960 puts a positive duty on anyone in charge of an animal to prevent unnecessary pain, so inaction is itself actionable. Section 11(1) then lists the offences: beating, kicking, overloading, starving, confining, abandoning and more. Basis PCA 1960 s.3 PCA 1960 s.11(1) A2 Which section carries a real sentence for cruelty? Where the animal is killed, poisoned, maimed or rendered useless, BNS Section 325 carries up to five years and is a cognizable offence, so the police are obliged to register an FIR rather than take a complaint and sit on it. It applies to any animal, owned or not, and the old value thresholds in IPC 428 and 429 are gone. Charge it there. The PCA Act alone is not worth filing under: its penalty has never been raised from the 1960 figures, and the 2022 amendment that would raise it is still not enacted. Careful Section 325 is mischief, so it needs an intentional act: starving, neglect and failure to treat are not mischief, and belong under PCA Section 11 read with Section 3. And it is bailable, so expect the accused to be released; the value of the section is that it forces registration and carries a real sentence at trial, not that it holds anyone. Basis PCA 1960 s.11(1) BNS 2023 s.325 A3 Is killing or maiming a dog a crime? Yes, and it is the serious charge. BNS Section 325, which replaced IPC 428 and 429, punishes killing, poisoning, maiming or rendering useless any animal with up to five years, or fine, or both. Do this Insist the FIR names Section 325 and not merely the PCA Act. Basis BNS 2023 s.325 A4 Can one be jailed for poisoning stray dogs? Yes. Section 11(1)(l) of the PCA Act names stray dogs expressly and prohibits killing them by strychnine or any other unnecessarily cruel method. Layer that with BNS Section 325 for the custodial sentence. Preserve the carcass for post mortem, because the toxicology report is the case. Basis PCA 1960 s.11(1)(l) BNS 2023 s.325 A5 What are the ABC Rules 2023? Rules framed under Section 38 of the PCA Act for managing community dogs: catch, sterilise, vaccinate and return the dog to the exact place it was picked up from. Return to the same locality is the rule, not a concession. The local body must run the programme through an AWBI recognised organisation. Basis ABC Rules 2023 PCA 1960 s.38 A6 Who is responsible for stray dogs in my area? The local body, meaning your municipal corporation, city municipal council or gram panchayat. The ABC Rules 2023 place the duty to run sterilisation and anti rabies vaccination on it, not on residents or feeders. If it has no ABC programme, that is a default you can act on in writing. Basis ABC Rules 2023 A7 Can stray dogs be relocated or killed? As a rule, no. The ABC Rules require the sterilised and vaccinated dog to go back where it came from, and relocation is not a lawful method of dog control. The Supreme Court order of 19 May 2026 carved out a narrow exception for sensitive premises such as schools, hospitals, sports complexes, bus stands and railway stations: dogs picked up there are sterilised, vaccinated and moved to a designated shelter rather than returned. Do this Read that as an exception, not a licence. Careful This is a continuing suo motu matter now monitored by every High Court, so check the current position before relying on it. Basis ABC Rules 2023 SC 19 May 2026 A8 What did the Supreme Court's May 2026 judgment say? That the ABC Rules remain the primary tool, that blanket culling stays prohibited, that dogs caught in sensitive premises need not be re-released there, that every district must have at least one working ABC centre, and that officials who ignore the directions face action. It also upheld the AWBI’s standard operating procedure, which is the document a municipality is actually working from. The mandatory district centre is the part most useful to citizens. Careful The proceedings continue and High Courts are monitoring compliance, so directions can move. Basis SC 19 May 2026 ABC Rules 2023 A9 Can a stray dog be euthanised? Only on three grounds under the 2026 directions: rabies, incurable illness causing suffering, or a dog shown to be dangerously aggressive. A resident complaint is not a ground. The act must be performed humanely by a registered veterinarian. Anything short of that is killing under BNS Section 325. Careful The judgment says “rabid”, not “laboratory confirmed”, and the safeguard it names is assessment by qualified veterinary experts. Ask for that assessment on record rather than for a lab report the order does not require. Basis SC 19 May 2026 PCA 1960 s.13 BNS 2023 s.325 A10 Is feeding stray dogs legal? Yes, and obstructing a feeder is the actionable conduct, not the feeding. The ABC Rules 2023 require resident associations and local bodies to designate feeding spots. The Delhi High Court in Dr Maya D. Chablani v. Radha Mittal (2021) held that community dogs have a right to food and that c

pages.title: Someone, not something | People for Animals
pages.description: What the science says about the animals we eat: memory, self-control, play and feeling in hens, pigs, cows and goats, with every claim sourced.
headings: The pig who played video games
What they know, learn and remember
What they feel, and how we can tell
pages.body: Someone, not something | People for Animals Every drive, camp and open day is free to attend ✕ Someone, not something. Sources What the science says about the animals we eat. Eight short chapters: memory, self-control, play and feeling, with a quiz at the end and the sources beneath it. Not a flock. Individuals. A hen keeps track of the faces of many individual flockmates, holds a stable place in a pecking order, and uses more than twenty distinct calls. In one study, hens chose to wait for a larger food reward rather than take a smaller one immediately, a form of self-control. She is someone, not something. See the evidence Face memory Recognition Hens recognise and remember individual flockmates, and hold a stable place in a pecking order that depends on knowing exactly who is who. A patient bird Self-control Given the choice, hens have opted to wait several seconds longer for a larger portion of food instead of taking a smaller one straight away. Mirror test Problem-solving Pigs shown food only as a reflection worked out where it really was: seven of eight walked straight to the hidden bowl rather than behind the mirror. Nest builders Motherhood Given straw and room, a sow spends the day before giving birth building a nest, a behaviour that has survived thousands of years of domestication. The pig who played video games In a 2021 study, four pigs learned to move a cursor with a joystick and hit on-screen targets, well above chance, using only their snouts. Pigs also use mirrors to find hidden food, and their grunts carry information about how they feel: software trained on thousands of recorded calls could tell positive from negative states with over 90% accuracy. Test yourself What they know, learn and remember Sources Cows Learning Heifers that worked out how to press a panel to open a gate showed rising heart rates and livelier movement than controls, a response researchers read as excitement at solving the task. Goats Memory Goats mastered a two-step puzzle box and still solved it ten months later. When a task becomes impossible, they turn to look at a nearby human, much as dogs do. Sheep Faces Sheep can learn the faces of about fifty other sheep and remember them for up to two years. They can also pick out familiar human faces from photographs. Horses Reading us Shown photographs of angry human faces, horses' heart rates rose and they looked with the left eye, the side linked to processing threats. Happy faces drew no such reaction. What they feel, and how we can tell Sources Play Positive welfare Calves, lambs and kids play more when well fed and unstressed, and play drops when conditions worsen. Researchers treat it as a sign an animal is doing well, not just surviving. Optimism Judgement bias Like people, animals in a poor state read ambiguous cues pessimistically. Calves tested after hot-iron disbudding were less likely to approach an uncertain cue, a measurable sign of a negative mood. Company Social bonds Isolated sheep show stress in behaviour, hormones and brain activity, and pictures of sheep faces alone reduce it. Horses groomed at the withers, where they groom each other, show lowered heart rates. Ear talk Body language Cows' ears hint at mood: gently stroked, they settle their ears into more relaxed positions. Goats, for their part, prefer looking at photographs of smiling human faces over angry ones. Things science did not expect → → Chicks a few days old watched small groups of objects move behind two screens, then reliably went to the screen hiding the larger number. They were tracking additions and subtractions of quantities up to five. Rugani and colleagues, 2009 When their chicks received a harmless puff of air, mother hens' heart rates rose, their eye temperature dropped, and they stood alert and called to the chicks. Their own bodies responded to their chicks' mild distress. Edgar and colleagues, 2011 Horses shown a photograph of a person with an angry expression later behaved more warily toward that same person, met in real life hours afterwards with a neutral face. They had remembered the emotion and attached it to the individual. Proops and colleagues, 2018 Current Biology Goats learned a two-step puzzle box, pulling a lever and then lifting it to release food. Ten months later, with no practice in between, most solved it again within about a minute. Briefer and colleagues, 2014 Frontiers in Zoology Who would you underestimate? Which of these animals can remember fifty faces for two years? Which one shows signs of excitement when it works out how to open a gate? Take the two-minute quiz and find out how much you already knew. Take the quiz Where this comes from Every claim on this page is drawn from peer-reviewed research in animal cognition and welfare science. Where the evidence is limited or debated, we say so. In 2014 the Supreme Court of India read the right to life in Article 21 to cover animals too, holding that they are entitled to live with intrinsic worth, honour and dignity. The same judgment brought the five freedoms into Indian law, alongside the duty of compassion for living creatures in Article 51A(g). Read the sources
